w: A life-size bronze Godzilla guards the gate where the 1954 original was shot on miniature sets with a man sweating inside a rubber suit. The lot stays closed to outsiders, but the statue and a mural of Seven Samurai faces still draw pilgrims to the birthplace of kaiju cinema.
s: Guarding the gate where Godzilla was born
why: Toho's Setagaya lot is where Ishiro Honda invented the kaiju genre in 1954, and the studio still marks the spot with its own monster.

w: Built in 1911 as a kabuki playhouse called Takadaza, this snow-country hall survived fires and decades of decline to become one of the oldest cinemas still screening films in Japan. Volunteers keep its wooden benches and single screen running, now a Registered Tangible Cultural Property.
s: Japan's oldest working movie theatre
why: It is one of Japan's oldest continuously operating cinemas, saved from demolition by local volunteers rather than a chain.

w: A working troglodyte hotel dug into a Berber pit dwelling, its courtyard and vaulted rooms became Luke Skywalker's home on Tatooine in the 1977 Star Wars and returned for the prequels decades later. Guests can still sleep in the cave rooms the crew used and spot leftover set dressing on the walls.
s: Luke Skywalker's underground childhood home
why: It is the single most recognisable Star Wars filming location still functioning as a normal, bookable hotel.

w: Red sandstone cliffs and wind-carved mesas gave Lawrence of Arabia its 1962 desertscapes and later stood in for Mars in The Martian and Prometheus, and for Jedha in Rogue One. Bedouin guides lead jeep tours past Lawrence's Spring, threading real desert life through decades of borrowed alien and Arabian skies.
s: The desert that played Mars, Tatooine and Arabia
why: Few landscapes have doubled for as many fictional worlds, from Lawrence's Arabia to two different Mars missions.

w: Opened in 1932 with what was then Cairo's largest screen, this Art Deco complex on Talaat Harb Street once broadcast state radio from its rooftop, giving the whole block its name. Chandeliers and a sweeping staircase front a hall that hosted Golden Age Egyptian film, now restored as a cultural venue.
s: Downtown Cairo's grandest 1932 movie palace
why: It anchors downtown Cairo's Art Deco cinema row and gave its name to the surrounding block.

w: A working sheep farm near Matamata became Bilbo Baggins's Shire for Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit, and unlike most blockbuster sets it was rebuilt in permanent materials rather than torn down. Forty-four hobbit holes sit in real pasture, ending at the Green Dragon Inn for a pint after the tour.
s: The Shire, still standing on a sheep farm
why: It is the rare film set kept permanently intact rather than demolished, turning a working farm into Middle-earth for good.

w: This road tunnel and the stone staircase above it mark the route the Kim family flees down through pouring rain in Parasite, tumbling from a wealthy hillside neighborhood toward their flooding home. Bong Joon-ho chose the site for its literal downward slope, mapping class onto Seoul's real altitude.
s: Parasite's downhill run to the flood
why: The tunnel's real topography let Bong Joon-ho stage his Oscar-winning film's central class metaphor without a single effect.

w: Opened by Mussolini in 1937 as fascist infrastructure, this backlot became Hollywood-on-the-Tiber in the 1950s for Roman Holiday and Ben-Hur, then Fellini's own dream factory for La Dolce Vita. Guided tours walk the soundstages and a permanent Ancient Rome street set, past ninety years of costumes.
s: Mussolini's studio, Fellini's playground
why: Few studios span both fascist-era spectacle and arthouse cinema history as directly as Cinecitta's soundstages.

w: Designed by Adolfo Morales de los Rios in Moorish-tinged Belle Epoque style, this 1906 theatre anchored Cinelandia, the strip of movie palaces that named the square, and became the first Rio cinema fitted for CinemaScope. It closed as a cinema in the 2000s and reopened restored in 2016 under a new name.
s: Rio's 1906 Belle Epoque picture palace
why: It is the last surviving grand hall from the strip of cinemas that gave Rio's Cinelandia square its name.

w: Running continuously since 1912, this is the oldest large-scale film studio on earth, where Fritz Lang built the towering city of Metropolis and Marlene Dietrich sang in The Blue Angel. The public Filmpark walks visitors past a 1929 soundstage built for Germany's first talkies and a permanent Berlin street set.
s: The world's oldest large-scale film studio
why: It has operated longer than any other major studio, spanning silent-era German Expressionism to modern co-productions.

w: Founded in the 1920s and built up on Sparrow Hills through the Soviet era, this studio produced Eisenstein's disciples and Andrei Tarkovsky's dreamlike epics before nearly collapsing after 1991. Daily tours now walk visitors through preserved backlot streets and a fleet of vintage cars used across decades of film.
s: The studio behind Battleship Potemkin's heirs
why: It is one of the world's oldest and largest studios, having shaped Soviet cinema from Eisenstein through Tarkovsky.

w: Set inside the restored Atlas Cinema in the historic Atlas Passage arcade, this museum resurrects Yesilcam, the Turkish film industry's mid-century golden age, with wax figures of its stars and vintage projectors. The cinema itself still screens films beneath the same ornate 1948 auditorium ceiling.
s: Yesilcam's golden age, preserved on Istiklal
why: It is the only museum dedicated to Yesilcam, the once-thriving Turkish studio system that rivaled regional cinema.

w: A crevassed tongue of Europe's largest ice cap, this glacier played Dr Mann's frozen alien world in Interstellar and the training grounds where Bruce Wayne learned to fear in Batman Begins. A short walk from the car park leads to blue ice ridges that also stood in for Hoth in Star Wars.
s: The ice planet from Interstellar
why: This single glacier tongue has doubled for at least three different fictional planets across major franchises.

w: Founded in 1983 in the desert light David Lean scouted for Lawrence of Arabia, this studio grew into the largest film lot on earth by area, its backlots holding leftover pharaonic temples, Roman colonnades, and Jerusalem streets from Gladiator, The Mummy, and Kingdom of Heaven.
s: The world's largest film studio by area
why: It is recognized as the world's largest film studio by land area, built on the desert light that first drew David Lean.

w: Carpenter Carlo Simi built this Wild West town for Sergio Leone's 1965 For a Few Dollars More, and it stayed standing to host The Good, the Bad and the Ugly the next year, cementing Almeria's badlands as spaghetti western country. Saloon shootout re-enactments still run daily along the same dusty main street.
s: The desert town Sergio Leone built
why: It is the surviving backlot that made Almeria's desert the default stand-in for the American West in 1960s Italian westerns.

w: Ingmar Bergman first came to this wind-scoured Baltic island in 1960 scouting locations and stayed forty years, shooting Persona, Shame, and Scenes from a Marriage among its limestone stacks and pine forests. His farmhouse now hosts writers and filmmakers in residence, with a nearby center running screenings.
s: The Baltic island where Bergman shot for decades
why: It is the actual home and working landscape of one of cinema's most influential directors, not a recreation.

w: Isak Dinesen's real farmhouse at the foot of the Ngong Hills, restored with 1980s film-set furniture donated after the 1985 Out of Africa production, sits in the Nairobi suburb still named Karen after her. The coffee plantation is gone, but the veranda and hills on the horizon match Sydney Pollack's sweeping shots.
s: The farm at the foot of the Ngong Hills
why: It blends the real writer's home with props from the Oscar-winning film it inspired, in a suburb named after her.

w: A whitewashed chapel perched alone on a sheer volcanic outcrop above the Aegean, reachable only by climbing roughly 200 rock-cut steps, this became Sophie's wedding church at the climax of Mamma Mia. The building predates the film by centuries and still holds services amid a steady stream of visitors humming ABBA.
s: The clifftop chapel from Mamma Mia's wedding
why: Its precarious clifftop setting made it the film's most photographed location and a pilgrimage site.

w: Francis Ford Coppola staged Apocalypse Now's helicopter beach assault here in 1976, and the surfboards his crew left behind sparked the surf culture that later made Baler the Philippines' unofficial surfing capital. Long-time locals still point out where the assault choppers came in low over the water.
s: Where the Ride of the Valkyries was filmed
why: A single wartime film shoot accidentally founded an entire local surf industry that still defines the town today.

w: Built from the mid-1990s around a full-scale replica of Beijing's Old Summer Palace, this rural studio complex grew into the largest outdoor film and television shooting base on earth, producing roughly a third of China's costume dramas. Extras in imperial armor mill between the reconstructed gates.
s: Chinawood, the world's largest outdoor lot
why: It is the largest film studio complex in the world by area, an entire town built to manufacture period drama.

w: Spread across roughly 2,000 acres outside Hyderabad, this Telugu-founded complex earned a Guinness listing as the world's largest film studio and produces Tollywood and Bollywood blockbusters alike, including the Baahubali sets still open to visitors. A replica London street draws daily crowds.
s: The largest film studio complex on record
why: It holds the Guinness World Record for largest film studio complex, doubling as both working lot and theme park.

w: Limestone karsts rise straight out of flooded rice paddies and river caves here, a landscape so otherworldly that Kong: Skull Island used it largely unaltered for the film's title island. Rowers still pole flat boats through the same passages, and the film sent tourism to this UNESCO site soaring.
s: The real Skull Island, by rowboat
why: The film crew barely needed special effects here, using a real UNESCO landscape to build an entire fictional island.

w: Rebuilt in the 1930s after three centuries as a ruin, this tidal-island castle at the meeting of three sea lochs became the fictional Scottish headquarters of MI6 in The World Is Not Enough and has stood in for Highlander and countless period dramas since.
s: Scotland's most photographed film castle
why: Its rebuilt-ruin silhouette has become cinema's default visual shorthand for the Scottish Highlands.

w: A volcanic outcrop of jumbled boulders and hidden clefts north of Melbourne, this rock formation gave Peter Weir's 1975 Picnic at Hanging Rock its eerie disappearance scene and became shorthand for Australian gothic unease. Walking trails now climb the same crevices the schoolgirls vanished into in the film.
s: Where three schoolgirls vanished on screen
why: It turned a real geological curiosity into the visual language of Australian gothic cinema for a generation.

w: Abbas Kiarostami shot Where Is the Friend's House? in this small Gilan village in 1987, then returned after a 1990 earthquake killed tens of thousands nearby to film Life, and Nothing More, weaving real rubble and survivors' tents into the story.
s: The mud-brick village of Kiarostami's trilogy
why: Kiarostami's return after a real earthquake turned a single village into a landmark of humanist filmmaking.

w: Opened in 1947 as the Warner on the Radiocentro complex, this modernist cinema was renamed Yara after the revolution and still glows red and blue over La Rampa, one of Havana's defining pieces of mid-century architecture. Its 1,650 seats have hosted the New Latin American Film Festival for decades.
s: Havana's neon-lit modernist movie palace
why: Its neon-lit modernist facade is one of Havana's most recognisable Cold War-era buildings and remains a working cinema.

w: Opened in 1945 through a deal with RKO, this studio became the production hub of Mexico's Golden Age cinema, churning out ranchero melodramas and comedies at a rate of dozens a year through the 1940s and 1950s. Nationalized in 1950, it later hosted Hollywood shoots from Titanic to Total Recall.
s: The engine room of Mexico's Golden Age
why: It anchored an entire national cinema's peak creative era and still produces most Mexican films made today.

w: Opened in 1916 inside a former pearling merchant's shed, this open-air picture garden still screens films under Broome's night sky between deckchairs and palm trees, the floor occasionally flooding at king tide. Believed to be the oldest continuously operating outdoor cinema in the world.
s: The world's oldest operating outdoor cinema
why: It is widely regarded as the oldest operating outdoor cinema on earth, still screening films exactly as it did in 1916.
